explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The text says that when Saul saw the Philistine army, he was afraid and trembled violently. That's not a king getting ready to charge. That's a king whose whole body is shaking like a cookie sheet someone just dropped.

Right, friend. When Saul saw the Philistine army, he was afraid and trembled violently. A king with a whole army gathered behind him, and his body is still doing its own thing. Afraid and shaking, that's the picture the text gives.

That's the one, friend. Saul inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him by dreams or Urim or prophets. Three ways Saul might have heard from Him, and none of them brought a word. I think that's a heavy moment, and Saul feels it.

explanations.answer: He answers Saul in a dream
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but the text says the opposite. The LORD did not answer Saul by dreams. Dreams are one of the ways named in the verse, and Saul gets nothing through any of them.

explanations.answer: He answers Saul through a prophet
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think so, friend, since Israel had prophets. But the text says the LORD did not answer Saul by prophets. Dreams, Urim and prophets are all named, and all three stay quiet for Saul.

You got it, baker. Saul tells his servants, “Find me a woman who is a medium, so I can go and consult her.” His servants answer that there is a medium at Endor. Saul had removed the mediums from the land (1 Samuel 28:3), so this request stands out.
That's a real word in the Bible, friend. Deborah, a leader in Israel, was a prophetess (Judges 4:4). But here Saul asks for a woman who is a medium. Then the servants point him to Endor.

The LORD did raise up judges in Israel (Judges 2:16), friend, but that's not who Saul asks for. He says, “Find me a woman who is a medium…” The servants answer with a medium at Endor, and that's where he heads.

Yes, friend. Saul disguises himself by putting on different clothes, and he sets out with two of his men. The text doesn't say why he does it, but I think a king in a costume is the kind of thing nobody forgets. I've worn my apron and chef's hat so long I'd never pull off a disguise.

That's a real thing in the Bible, friend, but this passage doesn't mention it. What the text says is that Saul disguised himself by putting on different clothes. He sets out with two of his men, and they come to the woman at night.

explanations.answer: He calls for Abiathar the priest
explanations.explanation: Abiathar was a priest (1 Samuel 23:9), friend, but he doesn't show up anywhere in this passage. Before Saul heads out, the text says he disguised himself by putting on different clothes. Then he set out with two of his men.

explanations.answer: She asks why he set a trap to get her killed
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. She says, “Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has killed the mediums and spiritists in the land. Why have you set a trap to get me killed?” Think about that. The disguise works so well that she's complaining about Saul to Saul.

explanations.answer: She asks to be paid in silver first
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention silver here, friend. What she does is remind Saul's disguised self of what Saul has done to the mediums and spiritists in the land. Then she asks why he has set a trap to get her killed.

explanations.answer: She tells him to come back tomorrow
explanations.explanation: No scheduling here, friend. She doesn't send him away until tomorrow. She says Saul has killed the mediums and spiritists in the land, and she asks why he has set a trap to get her killed.

That's right, friend. Saul swears to her by the LORD: “As surely as the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this.” She had just asked why he was setting a trap to get her killed, so he answers her fear with a promise.

Not this time, friend. The text says Saul did swear to her by the LORD: “As surely as the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this.” She had just asked why he'd set a trap to get her killed. That oath is his answer.

Yes, friend. The woman asks whom she should bring up, and Saul says, “Bring up Samuel…” Samuel, a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20), had already died and been buried in Ramah (1 Samuel 28:3). He's the one Saul asks for by name.

Eli was a priest in Israel (1 Samuel 1:9), friend, but he isn't who Saul asks for. Saul says, “Bring up Samuel…” Samuel is the prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20) who had died, and the passage tells us that at the start.

Moses, who was sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, friend, but he's not the one here. Saul says, “Bring up Samuel…” Samuel is a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20), and the passage said he had died.
Not quite, friend. The woman doesn't stay calm or quiet. The text says she cries out in a loud voice. Then she says to Saul, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!”
Right. When she sees Samuel, she cries out in a loud voice. Then she says to Saul, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!” Calm and quiet was not on the menu, friend.

explanations.answer: An old man wearing a robe
explanations.explanation: That's what she says, friend. “An old man is coming up…” she replies. “And he is wearing a robe.” Right after that, the text says Saul knew it was Samuel.

explanations.answer: A young man holding a spear
explanations.explanation: A spear would fit a battlefield, friend, but not this description. She says, “An old man is coming up…” Then she adds that he is wearing a robe, and Saul knows it is Samuel.

explanations.answer: A tall man dressed in armor
explanations.explanation: Armor makes sense with two armies camped nearby, friend, but she doesn't describe armor. She says an old man is coming up, and he is wearing a robe. Saul hears that and knows it was Samuel.
That's right, friend. Once Saul knew it was Samuel, he bowed facedown in reverence. This is the king who walked in wearing a disguise. Now he's flat on his face.
Not this time, friend. The text says that once Saul knew it was Samuel, he bowed facedown in reverence. The woman had already cried out, “You are Saul!” Now the king is on his face.
That's it, friend. Saul says the Philistines are fighting against him and God no longer answers him. Then he says, “So I have called on you to tell me what to do.” He wants a plan from Samuel.

explanations.answer: Pray to the LORD for him
explanations.explanation: That makes sense as a thing to ask, friend, but Saul doesn't ask for it. He says, “So I have called on you to tell me what to do.” What he wants is direction.
A blessing before battle sounds right, friend, but it's not on the table. Saul tells Samuel, “So I have called on you to tell me what to do.” He's asking for instructions.

Yes, friend. Samuel says the LORD has torn the kingdom out of Saul's hand and given it to his neighbor David. Samuel adds that the LORD has done exactly what He spoke through him. David is the name Samuel gives.
Jonathan was Saul's son (1 Samuel 14:49), friend, but he isn't the name Samuel gives. Samuel says the kingdom was given to “…your neighbor David.” David is the answer here.

Achish was the Philistine king of Gath (1 Samuel 27:2), friend, but he's not who Samuel names. Samuel says the LORD has torn the kingdom out of Saul's hand. The LORD gave it to “…your neighbor David.” It's David.

Not this one, friend. Samuel doesn't say Saul refused to fight the Philistines. He says it's because Saul did not obey the LORD or carry out His burning anger against Amalek. The reason has to do with Amalek.

Right, friend. Samuel says the LORD did this because Saul did not obey Him or carry out His burning anger against Amalek. Fighting the Philistines isn't the reason Samuel gives. The reason he names is about obeying the LORD.

That's right, friend. Samuel says the LORD will deliver Israel with Saul into the hand of the Philistines. He says it again about the army of Israel. It's a hard thing to hear, and I think it hits Saul hard.

Not this time, friend. Samuel does say it. He says the LORD will deliver Israel with Saul into the hand of the Philistines, and then he says the LORD will deliver the army of Israel into their hand as well.

explanations.answer: He falls flat on the ground
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Immediately Saul falls flat on the ground, terrified by the words of Samuel. The text also says his strength was gone because he hadn't eaten anything all that day and night. That's one tired, scared king.

explanations.answer: He draws his sword at Samuel
explanations.explanation: No sword comes out, friend. The text says Saul falls flat on the ground, terrified by Samuel's words. It also says his strength was gone, because he had not eaten anything all that day and night.

explanations.answer: He tears his robe and weeps
explanations.explanation: That's a way people show grief in the Bible, friend, but it's not what the text says here. Saul immediately falls flat on the ground. He's terrified by Samuel's words, and his strength is gone.

explanations.answer: Set some bread before him to eat
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. She asks to set a morsel of bread before him so he may eat and have the strength to go on his way. Saul hadn't eaten anything all that day and night. A woman offering bread gets my attention every time.

explanations.answer: Hide him in her house from the Philistines
explanations.explanation: That's not in the text, friend. She asks to set a morsel of bread before Saul so he may eat and have the strength to go on his way. It's a meal she offers.

explanations.answer: Send word to his army at Gilboa
explanations.explanation: Gilboa is where Saul camped with all Israel (1 Samuel 28:4), friend, but she doesn't offer to send word there. What she offers is a morsel of bread, so Saul can eat and have the strength to go on his way. It's a meal, nothing more.
Not so fast, friend. Saul refuses. He says, “I will not eat.” After all that, he still turns down the bread.
Right, friend. Saul refuses, saying, “I will not eat.” He doesn't give in until his servants join the woman in urging him. Then he heeds their voice.
That's right, friend. Saul's servants join the woman in urging him to eat. Saul had first said, “I will not eat.” After they urged him, the text says he heeded their voice.
Samuel did mention Saul's sons, friend, when he said that tomorrow Saul and his sons will be with him. But they're not the ones urging him here. The text says his servants join the woman.
No elders show up in this scene, friend. The text says Saul's servants join the woman in urging him. After that, Saul heeds their voice.
Yes, friend. The text says that night they got up and left. They came to the woman at night (1 Samuel 28:8), so the whole visit happens in the dark. Full of bread, off they go.
Not morning, friend. The text says that night they got up and left. They had come to the woman at night too (1 Samuel 28:8), so the visit stays in the dark.
No afternoon here, friend. The text says that night they got up and left. Saul had arrived at night too (1 Samuel 28:8), so the whole visit is after dark.
